paragraphs: This paper develops a simplex algorithm for linear programs arising from a linear classification formulation. The central question is how efficiently this particular kind of optimization problem can be solved. Rather than treating classification as an arbitrary linear program, the analysis focuses on its margin, which the abstract identifies as the main parameter governing complexity.

The authors prove that, for margin values they describe as practically relevant, their simplex variant needs only a polylogarithmic number of pivot steps in the worst case. Pivot steps are the successive moves made by the simplex procedure. The paper also establishes near-linear overall running time, so its efficiency claim concerns both the number of these moves and the total computation.

The significance is a strong complexity guarantee for a structured classification setting. The abstract contrasts this result with general linear programming, where no sub-polynomial pivot rule is known. The margin qualification is essential: the result establishes favorable behavior for the stated classification regime, rather than a general solution to the complexity of simplex methods.
neurips-2012-a-polylog-pivot-steps-simpl.tldr: A simplex variant achieves polylogarithmic worst-case pivot counts and near-linear running time for linear classification with practically relevant margins.

paragraphs: This paper connects an efficient optimization building block with a method for accelerating convex minimization. Its starting point is the proximity calculation, an operation used within proximal optimization methods. The authors develop efficient implementations for a useful class of functions, making this calculation the foundation for the larger optimization procedure.

The computational opportunity comes from the corresponding dual problem having a piecewise-linear structure. The implementations exploit that structure to carry out the proximity calculation efficiently. In the second part of the work, the authors use this result to construct a quasi-Newton method for convex minimization. The two contributions therefore fit together: improving the underlying calculation enables the proposed acceleration method.

The abstract reports that the resulting optimization method compares favorably with leading alternatives. It also identifies a broad range of applications, including signal processing, sparse regression and recovery, machine learning, and classification. The contribution matters because a reusable improvement to an optimization operation can support several different problem types, with the reported comparisons providing evidence for the resulting method's practical value.
neurips-2012-a-quasi-newton-proximal-spl.tldr: Efficient proximity calculations based on a piecewise-linear dual problem enable a competitive quasi-Newton method for convex optimization.

paragraphs: The paper proposes approximate inference for a broad class of non-conjugate probabilistic models. The task is to represent a target probability density with another density that is easier to work with. Its specific development concerns target densities from generalized linear models, giving a concrete model family within the broader inference problem.

The authors introduce a rich family of variational approximating densities. They select the approximation by minimizing Kullback-Leibler divergence, which supplies the criterion for how closely a candidate should match the target. This makes the choice of approximation an optimization problem: the method searches within its proposed family for the best fit according to that criterion.

The key computational ingredient is a Fourier representation, which the authors show leads to efficient and scalable inference. The contribution therefore combines flexibility in the approximation with a representation that makes fitting it tractable. The stated result concerns approximate inference in the described model setting; its value is an approach for handling non-conjugate targets while retaining a rich set of possible approximations.
neurips-2012-affine-independent-variatio.tldr: A Fourier-based variational method supports efficient, scalable approximate inference for generalized linear model target densities.

paragraphs: Clinical trial blinding aims to conceal which intervention participants receive because their expectations can interact with the intervention's effects. The paper starts from the difficulty of ensuring or verifying perfect blinding. It examines the practice of asking participants afterward which intervention they believe they received, converting their answers into a blinding score, and applying a pass-or-fail threshold.

The authors identify fundamental problems with this practice and discuss them in relation to commonly used blinding measures. They then propose a different method for handling trials whose blinding is imperfect. Their approach still uses a questionnaire after the trial, so the central change is how participants' responses are interpreted and used.

The proposed interpretation avoids ad hoc adjustable parameters and is reported to be robust to small changes in the questionnaire data. It also does not rely on strong assumptions for interpreting participants' feedback. These properties address weaknesses in judging a trial through a thresholded blinding score and provide a different way to use evidence about participants' beliefs when blinding is incomplete.
neurips-2012-assessing-blinding-in-clini.tldr: The paper critiques threshold-based blinding assessments and proposes a robust, parameter-free interpretation of post-trial participant feedback.

paragraphs: Pedigree analysis uses family relationships to identify genomic sites associated with disease. The paper addresses a mismatch between expanding genetic datasets and analysis methods restricted to relatively small family trees. It also questions the flexibility of traditional linkage log-odds estimators, which are difficult to interpret and extend to interactions between genomic sites.

The authors introduce a formalism for expressing genetic disease models, drawing on graphical model inference and transducer theory. They show how models written in this formalism can become accurate, efficient estimators. A central part of the approach is constructing a variational approximation that makes the inference problem computationally manageable.

The method enables analysis of larger pedigrees than those previously analyzed in the literature, and the abstract reports improved prediction of disease-associated sites. Its contribution links richer disease modeling with the ability to use larger family structures. The authors also suggest that their approximation technique could apply to other large graphical models, presenting that broader use as a possibility rather than an established result.
neurips-2012-bayesian-pedigree-analysis-.tldr: A disease-modeling formalism and variational inference method enable larger pedigree analyses and improve disease-site prediction.

paragraphs: Warped Gaussian processes model regression observations through a nonlinear transformation of a Gaussian process. This transformation is part of the probability model and can provide a better prior description of the data. Earlier warped Gaussian processes used a parametric transformation and learned its parameters by maximum likelihood.

This paper replaces that transformation with a nonparametric one and uses variational inference to integrate it out. The change concerns both flexibility and treatment of the transformation: instead of relying on a single maximum-likelihood fit of its parameters, the Bayesian construction incorporates it through approximate integration. The authors show that this combination is possible within the warped Gaussian process framework.

The resulting model works in settings where the maximum-likelihood version failed, including limited data, censored observations, and classification. The paper also reports superior performance on several real datasets. These findings support the value of changing how the nonlinear transformation is modeled and handled, with benefits demonstrated across the stated settings rather than asserted for every prediction problem.
neurips-2012-bayesian-warped-gaussian-pr.tldr: Bayesian warped Gaussian processes integrate out a nonparametric transformation and succeed in settings where maximum-likelihood warping failed.

paragraphs: Distributed optimization divides work among processors, but coordinating them takes time. This paper asks how many processors a problem should use and how often they should communicate when communication has a cost. Its analysis centers on a problem-dependent quantity, r, that summarizes the tradeoff between communication and computation.

The communication pattern changes the scaling behavior. Organizing processors through a regular expander graph produces speedups in the analysis. When every processor communicates with every other processor, there is instead an optimal processor count that depends on r. This makes network organization part of the optimization design, alongside the amount of computing hardware.

The paper also shows that reducing communication frequency as computation progresses can shorten the time needed to reach a fixed accuracy. More frequent coordination is therefore not always the fastest route to that target. Experiments on a real cluster, using metric learning and nonsmooth convex minimization problems, closely agree with the theoretical results and support their practical relevance.
neurips-2012-communication-computation-t.tldr: Communication topology and progressively less frequent coordination can improve distributed optimization speed when communication is costly.

paragraphs: A graphical model's density of states describes how many configurations have each likelihood value. This paper introduces Density Propagation, a message-passing method for estimating that function. Tracking this richer information provides a way to study the distribution of configuration values rather than only obtaining an aggregate quantity.

The authors show that Density Propagation is exact on tree-structured graphical models and strictly generalizes both sum-product and max-product algorithms. They then combine density-of-states information with tree decomposition to derive upper and lower bounds on the partition function. The method thus connects a new inference procedure with guarantees about a central quantity in probabilistic models.

For any tree decomposition, the proposed upper bound is provably at least as tight as earlier bounds based on convexity of the log-partition function. It is strictly tighter when a stated general condition holds. Experiments also show improvements over convex-relaxation and mean-field bounds. The distinction matters: the theoretical comparison guarantees no loss in tightness, while strict improvement has an additional condition.
neurips-2012-density-propagation-and-imp.tldr: Density Propagation estimates configuration-value counts and yields partition-function bounds with a provably no-weaker upper bound than earlier convexity-based bounds.

paragraphs: Entangled Monte Carlo addresses the communication cost of running sequential Monte Carlo algorithms across multiple machines. Such simulations work with particles, and moving those particles between machines can be expensive. The proposed method changes what must travel across the network by reconstructing particles from their genealogy instead of transmitting the particles themselves.

The authors show how communication can be reduced to particle weights for each machine while keeping the parallel simulation globally coherent in an implicit form. They also describe efficient ways to maintain the genealogy so that any particle can be reconstructed. This makes the ancestry information an operational part of the simulation, supporting reconstruction when particle information is needed.

Experiments in Bayesian phylogenetics show that the computational benefit from parallelization substantially exceeds the reconstruction cost. Timing results also indicate that reconstructing particles is much more efficient than transmitting them in those examples. The practical finding is that additional local reconstruction work can be worthwhile when it replaces costly communication while preserving a coordinated simulation.
neurips-2012-entangled-monte-carlo-4ce76.tldr: Entangled Monte Carlo reduces parallel simulation communication by reconstructing particles from genealogy, with favorable timing results in Bayesian phylogenetics.

paragraphs: Multi-label classification allows an example to belong to several classes, making prediction costly when the label space is large. Label-space dimension reduction addresses this by using a smaller representation of the labels. The paper observes that existing approaches build that representation from labels alone, leaving out the input features that will be used to predict them.

The proposed conditional principal label space transformation uses both features and labels. It is derived by minimizing an upper bound on Hamming loss, tying the reduced representation to a criterion for label-prediction errors. The required minimization can be performed efficiently through singular value decomposition, giving the approach a direct computational procedure.

The method also has a kernelized extension, which lets more sophisticated combinations of features inform label-space reduction. Experiments across many real datasets find it more effective than existing reduction approaches. The central contribution is to make label compression sensitive to the information available in the inputs, with the reported results supporting that choice for multi-label prediction.
neurips-2012-feature-aware-label-space-d.tldr: Conditional principal label space transformation uses features and labels to build an efficient reduced label representation with improved empirical effectiveness.

paragraphs: Statistical network models often begin with strong assumptions about the properties a graph should exhibit. The paper highlights the difficulty this creates when those properties are unknown beforehand. A model designed around a particular degree distribution, for example, may be poorly suited to a domain whose network behavior has not already been characterized.

The authors introduce the Fiedler delta statistic, built from the graph Laplacian spectrum. It allows them to avoid parametric assumptions about the network properties being modeled. They use this statistic to construct Fiedler random fields, a model intended to estimate edge distributions efficiently in large random networks.

The paper analyzes the dependence structure of these random fields and fits them to several real networks. In those evaluations, it reports substantially higher modeling accuracy than other established statistical approaches. The contribution joins flexibility in describing network properties with efficient estimation at scale. Its empirical results indicate that this combination can improve network modeling when a predetermined property-specific distribution is an unsuitable starting point.
neurips-2012-fiedler-random-fields-a-lar.tldr: Fiedler random fields use a spectral graph statistic to estimate large-network edge distributions without parametric assumptions about modeled properties.

paragraphs: This paper studies how prediction error changes as multi-task Gaussian process regression receives more examples. Its learning curves track the average Bayes error for one task against the total training examples across all tasks. The analysis assumes a covariance formed by multiplying an input covariance function with a freely specified matrix of relationships between tasks.

For this model family, the authors obtain accurate learning-curve approximations for any number of tasks and investigate behavior with large amounts of data. They find that multi-task learning can become essentially unhelpful asymptotically: examples from other tasks help only when inter-task correlation is close to its maximum. This effect is strongest for smooth target functions, such as those described by squared exponential kernels.

With many tasks, the curves exhibit two phases. Collective learning initially lowers errors toward a plateau even though most tasks have no examples. A later decline occurs only when the example count becomes proportional to the task count. These findings distinguish early benefits from sharing information from the conditions needed for continued improvement.
neurips-2012-learning-curves-for-multi-t.tldr: Learning-curve analysis shows early collective benefits but potentially negligible asymptotic gains from multi-task Gaussian process regression unless tasks are highly correlated.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to recover a hidden transmission network from event cascades. In settings involving information, disease, or influence, observations may reveal when events happened without revealing the connections that carried them. The learning problem is therefore to infer network structure using only the timestamps recorded across cascades.

A central difficulty is that influence can differ substantially between pairs of entities. The authors argue that a simple parametric model cannot describe this heterogeneity adequately. They propose a kernel-based approach that can represent a diverse range of influence types without requiring a predetermined form for those influences. This flexibility is built into the network-discovery method.

Evaluations on synthetic and real cascade data show better recovery of the underlying diffusion network and substantially improved estimates of the influence functions between entities. These are complementary outcomes: one concerns which connections exist, while the other concerns how influence behaves along them. The results support using flexible influence models when reconstructing networks whose transmission behavior varies across relationships.
neurips-2012-learning-networks-of-hetero.tldr: A kernel-based method learns hidden diffusion networks from cascade timestamps while accommodating heterogeneous influence between entities.

paragraphs: Latent factor models describe high-dimensional observations through a smaller set of hidden factors. This paper studies how to learn relationships among those factors as part of the representation itself. It proposes a general framework that encourages a sparse undirected graphical model over the latent factor vector, making pairwise dependencies an explicit learning target.

The specific model, SLFA, is formulated as matrix factorization with a regularization term that encourages collaborative reconstruction. Its central capability is simultaneous learning: it obtains a lower-dimensional data representation while also modeling pairwise relationships among the hidden factors. An online learning algorithm makes the approach feasible for large-scale problems.

Experiments use two synthetic datasets and two real datasets. The authors report that the learned factors and their relationships offer a more structured way to explore high-dimensional data, while the representations achieve state-of-the-art classification performance. These findings connect the model's explicit dependency structure with both data exploration and predictive usefulness in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2012-learning-the-dependency-str.tldr: SLFA jointly learns compact data representations and sparse pairwise dependencies among latent factors, with an online algorithm for large-scale learning.

paragraphs: Joint image alignment reduces unwanted variation, such as differences in pose, that can interfere with recognition. Earlier unsupervised methods for complex images depended on carefully chosen handcrafted descriptors to make alignment optimization behave well. This paper combines unsupervised alignment with unsupervised feature learning so that the representation adapts to the images being aligned.

The authors incorporate deep learning into the congealing alignment framework. Different network depths provide features at different resolutions, while learning tunes those features to the dataset's statistics. They also add a group sparsity penalty to restricted Boltzmann machine training, producing a topographic organization of learned filters and improving the subsequent alignment results.

On Labeled Faces in the Wild, images aligned by the proposed method produce significantly better face-verification accuracy than original images and earlier unsupervised and supervised alignment approaches. The method also matches the best available unpublished approach reported in the abstract. These results show the value of learning the feature representation alongside alignment in the tested face-recognition setting.
neurips-2012-learning-to-align-from-scra.tldr: Combining deep feature learning with unsupervised joint alignment improves face verification on Labeled Faces in the Wild.

paragraphs: Partition functions appear in probabilistic modeling, including conditional random fields, graphical models, and maximum-likelihood estimation. This paper introduces a quadratic variational upper bound to support optimization involving them. The bound enables majorization: repeatedly replacing a difficult optimization step with a simpler subproblem built from an upper-bounding function.

The computational usefulness of the bound extends to graphical models with small tree-width and to latent-likelihood settings. The small-tree-width qualification identifies a setting in which computing the bound remains efficient. For larger problems, the authors also develop low-rank versions, adapting the same basic strategy to situations where a full representation would be more costly.

Several learning applications lead to fast update rules with convergence properties. The abstract reports that the low-rank methods outperform LBFGS and first-order alternatives, and that experiments show advantages over leading optimization methods. The contribution is both an inequality that makes majorization possible and practical optimization procedures whose reported results support using that bound in probabilistic learning.
neurips-2012-majorization-for-crfs-and-l.tldr: A quadratic variational upper bound enables efficient majorization updates for probabilistic learning, with low-rank variants showing strong optimization results.

paragraphs: Multi-task learning traditionally minimizes the average empirical risk across tasks. This paper asks what happens when the objective pays more attention to the task with the largest error. It introduces minimax multi-task learning, which minimizes the maximum of the individual tasks' empirical risks, changing how performance across tasks is combined into one objective.

A relaxation of the minimax formulation creates a continuum between that worst-task objective and classical average-risk learning. The authors place these formulations inside a broader framework that operates on the vector of task risks. This framework includes the endpoints, their intermediate relaxations, and additional ways to compose task losses.

The theoretical result concerns learning to learn, where evaluation involves newly sampled tasks. In that setting, minimax learning tends to avoid worst-case outcomes. Experiments with several formulations on synthetic and real problems yield encouraging results in both multi-task and learning-to-learn settings. The contribution offers a way to express different priorities across tasks without committing exclusively to average performance.
neurips-2012-minimax-multi-task-learning.tldr: A generalized multi-task objective connects average-risk learning with minimax learning, which tends to avoid worst-case outcomes on newly sampled tasks.

paragraphs: A two-sample test asks whether two groups of observations provide evidence that their underlying distributions differ. This paper focuses on tests using maximum mean discrepancy, which compares distribution embeddings defined by a kernel. Because the kernel determines the comparison, its choice affects the test's ability to detect a real difference.

The authors propose choosing kernel parameters to maximize test power at a given test level. The level bounds the probability of falsely declaring a difference, while greater power reduces the chance of missing one that exists. This ties parameter selection directly to the statistical purpose of the test rather than relying on an earlier kernel-selection heuristic.

Computing the statistic, determining its threshold, and optimizing kernel parameters all have cost linear in sample size. These properties make the procedure suitable for streams whose observations cannot all remain in memory. Experiments show greater power than earlier selection heuristics, supporting the value of optimizing the kernel for detection while keeping the overall testing procedure scalable.
neurips-2012-optimal-kernel-choice-for-l.tldr: Power-focused kernel selection improves large-scale MMD two-sample tests while keeping selection and testing costs linear in sample size.

paragraphs: Relational datasets record connections among entities, often in arrays representing graphs, networks, databases, or matrices. The paper seeks a summary of the common structure behind those relationships. Its modeling basis is exchangeability: the relevant distribution is invariant to the ordering of rows and columns, so arbitrary ordering does not determine the modeled structure.

Probability results described in the abstract represent exchangeable arrays through a random measurable function. The authors treat that function as the parameter of a Bayesian model and place a Gaussian process prior on it. This yields a flexible Bayesian nonparametric model grounded in the representation of relational data through functions.

For efficient inference, the approach combines elliptical slice sampling with a random sparse approximation to the Gaussian process. The paper demonstrates applications to network data and explains connections to existing models, several of which arise as special cases. Its contribution is a simple, flexible modeling construction that also unifies established approaches within a broader function-based view of relational structure.
neurips-2012-random-function-priors-for-.tldr: A Gaussian process prior on the function representing an exchangeable array yields a flexible Bayesian model for networks and relational data.

paragraphs: The paper connects two approaches to decision-making over time. A robust Markov decision process evaluates decisions against unfavorable choices of uncertain model parameters. A risk-sensitive Markov decision process instead assumes known parameters and evaluates cumulative cost through a risk measure. The authors identify settings in which these seemingly different objectives are mathematically equivalent.

The first equivalence concerns minimizing expected exponential utility. This risk-sensitive objective corresponds to minimizing worst-case expected cost while penalizing deviations from nominal parameters. The penalty is measured by Kullback-Leibler divergence. Thus, in this formulation, sensitivity to risk can also be interpreted as protection against model changes whose departures from the nominal model carry a cost.

The second equivalence concerns iterated risk measures constructed from certain coherent risk measures. These correspond to robust objectives whose permitted parameter deviations are described through a concave function. Together, the results give precise connections between attitudes toward uncertain outcomes and uncertainty about model parameters. Their scope depends on the specified utility, risk measures, and descriptions of parameter deviations.
neurips-2012-robustness-and-risk-sensiti.tldr: The paper establishes equivalences between specified risk-sensitive MDP objectives and robust MDPs with corresponding penalties or constraints on parameter deviations.

paragraphs: Network communities can overlap, so an entity may participate in more than one group. This paper develops an algorithm for inferring such community structure in large networks using the mixed-membership stochastic blockmodel. The focus is posterior inference: estimating community memberships within the probabilistic model at a scale that makes existing inference computationally demanding.

The algorithm uses stochastic variational inference and interleaves network subsampling with updates to the estimated community structure. This connects learning from selected portions of the network with the ongoing inference process. The computational design makes subsampling an integral part of estimating overlapping memberships across the full network.

The authors apply the method to ten real networks containing as many as 60,000 nodes and find hundreds of communities. It converges several orders of magnitude faster than the leading MMSB algorithm used for comparison. Across 280 benchmark networks, community detection is at least as accurate as other scalable methods. These results support substantial computational gains alongside competitive recovery of community structure.
neurips-2012-scalable-inference-of-overl.tldr: Stochastic variational inference with network subsampling greatly accelerates overlapping-community inference while retaining competitive benchmark accuracy.

paragraphs: Labeled images may provide insufficient guidance for learning features in difficult visual recognition tasks. Semantic taxonomies can add relationships between object categories, but a single hierarchy may miss useful connections or include irrelevant ones. This paper combines multiple taxonomies so that different semantic views can contribute to recognizing each class.

For every taxonomy, the method learns a tree of semantic kernels. Each node contains a Mahalanobis kernel trained to distinguish the classes represented by its children. The resulting collection of trees forms a semantic kernel forest. The method then learns a separate combination of kernels for each class, selecting relationships that are useful for recognizing that particular category.

A hierarchical regularization term guides the combination weights using the taxonomies' structure. Experiments on challenging object-recognition datasets show significant accuracy improvements from combining the different views. The approach matters because it turns semantic relationships into selectable recognition features: multiple hierarchies supply candidate information, and class-specific learning determines which parts contribute to the visual task.
neurips-2012-semantic-kernel-forests-fro.tldr: Semantic kernel forests learn class-specific combinations of information from multiple taxonomies, improving accuracy on challenging object-recognition datasets.

paragraphs: Clustering depends on deciding which objects are similar. Crowdclustering uses human annotations to define those similarities, but its reliance on annotations limits it to objects that have been labeled. This paper proposes semi-crowdsourced clustering, which combines object features with crowd annotations for only a subset of the data.

The key step is learning a similarity measure over low-level features from the annotated portion. Once learned, that measure can be applied to objects without their own manual annotations. The authors address noise and differences between crowd workers through a metric-learning algorithm based on matrix completion, making inconsistent human judgments part of the learning problem.

An empirical study on two real image datasets finds that the proposed algorithm outperforms leading distance-metric learning methods in both clustering accuracy and computational efficiency. The contribution is a way to extend the usefulness of a limited annotation effort across a larger collection. The reported results support learning a feature-based similarity from imperfect crowd feedback instead of requiring annotations for every object.
neurips-2012-semi-crowdsourced-clusterin.tldr: Semi-crowdsourced clustering learns a robust feature-based similarity from partial crowd annotations so that unannotated objects can also be clustered.

paragraphs: The paper studies hidden linear dynamical systems whose observations follow non-Gaussian models. Its motivating application is neural population activity, where spike counts are Poisson-distributed and their log-rates depend on a latent dynamical process. That process may also receive external inputs. The goal is to estimate the underlying system parameters efficiently.

The authors extend spectral learning, also called subspace identification in this setting, beyond Gaussian observations. They show that the extended algorithm is consistent and accurately recovers parameters on large simulated datasets. Because it is non-iterative, it has much lower computational cost than approximate expectation-maximization in the reported comparisons.

On smaller datasets, the method also serves as an effective initialization for expectation-maximization, improving robustness and speeding convergence. The paper reports that these benefits extend to real neural recordings. The results therefore support two uses of the same estimator: direct parameter recovery with sufficient data and a computationally useful starting point for iterative fitting when data are more limited.
neurips-2012-spectral-learning-of-linear.tldr: Extended spectral identification efficiently estimates linear dynamics from non-Gaussian observations and improves EM initialization for neural population models.

paragraphs: This paper introduces divergence measures for sets, which can also be represented as binary vectors. The construction starts from tight modular upper or lower bounds on a submodular function, producing two kinds of submodular-Bregman divergence. The authors show that their properties parallel those of continuous Bregman divergences.

The framework generalizes several familiar measures, including weighted Hamming distance, weighted precision and recall, conditional mutual information, and a generalized set-based KL divergence. The paper also connects the discrete construction to a continuous one: applying generalized Bregman divergence to the Lovász extension yields the Lovász-Bregman divergence, which extends a submodular-Bregman divergence.

These connections support applications in optimization and clustering. A proximal algorithm based on the discrete divergence provides a framework for multiple mirror-descent-style methods for submodular optimization. A generalized k-means procedure using the continuous divergence suits clustering problems where ordering matters. In that procedure, the mean ordering is particularly efficient to compute, addressing a computational difficulty associated with other order-based distance measures.
neurips-2012-submodular-bregman-and-the-.tldr: Submodular-Bregman divergences unify set-based dissimilarities and connect to efficient optimization and order-sensitive clustering through the Lovász extension.
